This study focuses on enhancing the basic BiCGSTAF method by creating a new variant that removes the standard final step and instead incorporates a corrective factor to enhance solution accuracy. Building on this concept, we introduce an improved FGMRE method, known as I$^{2}$-FGMRES, by integrating a novel polishing stage after an I$^{2}$-BiCGSTAF iteration. Our research involves developing and analyzing these methods and conducting extensive numerical experiments to compare their performance. Furthermore, we present an adaptive approach to determine the optimal value of the corrective factor, demonstrating significant success in solving large-scale sparse linear systems with both theoretical and practical applications.

A critical challenge in surgery is accurately registering an organ's model to the real patient, and this accuracy can be compromised by the significant amount of noise generated by surgical tools. This project aims to improve real-time data registration by developing a method that automatically reduces denoising where deformations are high. A new, simple and effective network is proposed, and this study demonstrates its effectiveness through a variety of simulations and experiments using ultrasound data.

Deep neural networks are now widely used in real-time traffic management systems due to their efficiency in occlusion handling and safety enhancements for autonomous vehicles.
However, current occlusion-filling methods are trained using models that rely on accurate scene understanding. The presence of moving vehicles and hidden ground areas, which are inaccessible, pose challenges for self-supervised learning.
To address this challenge, we propose a novel occlusion filling dataset containing occluded scenes and corresponding masks, which we release for public use.
This dataset, which we evaluated our existing model on, demonstrates significant performance drops when dealing with larger occlusions. Consequently, it provides a clear path for improving occlusion filling techniques through rigorous, self-supervised training that accounts for complex scene dynamics, hidden ground areas, and filled patches.
Our work aims to guide future research in developing deep learning models that function effectively in these scenarios, which are essential for real-world applications.

Deep neural networks excel at pattern recognition but are dependent on specific tasks for each new classification problem. We introduce a novel neural network architecture with endurable low power consumption that functions across diverse classification tasks. Our network combines analog components for multiplication and active signal switching for all operations to minimize energy expenditure, and it uses a dynamic threshold mechanism to achieve efficient real-time decision-making. Experimental results show significant energy savings of over ten times and speed increases exceeding fifty times in relation to existing methods, and when tested on nine distinct classification tasks, our network delivered competent performance.

This research investigates how strong magnetic fields impact the structure of spin-polarized strange quark matter, specifically focusing on the general properties, mass density phases, and the characteristics of deconfined strange quark matter in these extreme conditions. We developed a "four-body" model to describe the dynamics of this matter under the influence of strong magnetic fields, considering the interactions between four fundamental components of the "f_0(980)", "K^*", "K", and kaons. We then examined the behavior of this matter by studying its equation of state, exploring how strong magnetic fields can lead to different, lighter mass states and ultimately, a transition to deconfined strange quark matter at various mass densities. Notably, we found that the characteristics of this matter, including its characteristics fermion, can give rise to different, highly charged, and rapidly spinning stars with masses and charges in the range of two to six times 10$^{21}$ kilograms and up to thirty billion coulombs, respectively. These findings may help explain the observations of strange quark matter and provide a framework for understanding the formation of these enigmatic objects.

A cubic graph is even-2-factorable if and only if it can be decomposed into distinct spanning subgraphs, specifically cycles, with an even number of edges. In 1967, Stein showed that every snark, a specific type of cubic graph, is not E2F. This study proves the existence of a new class of cubic graphs that are not even-2-factorable, which is characterized by its properties including being non-bridged, having an edge chromatic number of four, and possessing an irreducible cyclic colouring. Furthermore, this class of graphs is shown to be E2F, in contrast to the variety of characterized classes of graphs with an edge chromatic number of four, some of which are even-2-factorable.

Our new application analyzer, called Timeloops, aims to efficiently limit applications' access to specific system calls by manipulating process creation commands. Unlike previous methods, it can limit access for applications written in interpreted languages, including PHP and Python, without modifying the original source code. By using dynamic bytecode manipulation, it can accurately predict process creation command usage in complex code structures. Furthermore, it exhibits comparable performance to time-limiting process creation commands without additional constraints, making it an optimal process access-limiting solution for applications.

When attempting to track targets that have not been detected within a restricted field of view, our goal is to minimize a complex measure of how far targets could be from their true positions, given the unpredictable movements of multiple mobile sensors. Because the fields of view often result in a complex relationship between the sensor positions and the visibility of targets, our first step involved rephrasing the initial optimization problem to decouple this non-linear element, allowing us to accurately calculate the growth rate of the measurement's complexity with increasing numbers of targets. subsequently, we present a method to track the positions of undetected targets, even those never before observed, by using an modified version of the optimistic as-pis-off algorithm. This algorithm's design allows it to achieve the desired fields of view tracking performance, achieving a growth rate of computational complexity that is directly proportional to the measurement of the fields of view's increase.

This research aims to apply the concept of observability inequality to achieve a specific goal of population elimination within the model's species. To accomplish this, we first establish an observability inequality for the species in question, provided its population is monitored in a particular region during a sufficient amount of time. This condition is directly related to the species' natural habitat. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the observability inequality implies the ability to achieve extinction of the species, under the assumption that its population can be controlled in a specific manner.

We use our improved version of the Soccer-B environment, where we've revised the reward system to better reflect nuanced situations, for instance, by assigning positive reward for actions like committing a foul or causing the ball to go out, and instance-specific goals, for example, goalies saving goals with the ball in the penalty area, to demonstrate our approach to setting goals and evaluating policies in complex, dynamic team sports. Through our experiments, we find that defensive players can effectively learn to prioritize ball possession, by simulating full matches and evaluating policies by tracking the distribution of ball possession. Additionally, we observe that our environment and task-set allow us to gather a large dataset, for example, 100,000 steps can be completed in about 10 minutes, and that saving the state as late as possible yields the most benefits due to the non-stationary nature of the game. Finally, we provide video recordings of simulated matches to visually illustrate the matches' progress and the effects of different state-saving intervals on the matches' duration and quality.

A common issue with full waveform inversion is the circular process of updating the model and shifting wavefields to a different time step, which can be inefficient and less precise. This study introduces an alternative approach for full waveform inversion based on adjusting the time step of the updatables, which allows for simultaneous consideration of multiple time steps and reduces the problem to a smaller search space. This method is particularly efficient for large-scale full waveform inversion problems, as it combines the advantages of focusing on data misfit with a reduced model complexity. Our results, which combine an adaptive time step method with full waveform inversion, are obtained rapidly and with reduced precision, as shown in the geological model from well log data with seismic data.

When a set of sites, arranged in a grid, each contain a species of one of two types, and and and external pressures cause types to switch randomly, the competition between the two species can lead to three potential results. The outcomes vary from the complete extinction of one or both species to the persistence of both types in an asymptotic state. The range of long-term behavior also includes an phase where the distribution of persistent sites is finite. The scope of this model extends to include scenarios where the distribution is infinite, including the asymmetric case, where the type-swapping probability differs significantly across the site set. The asymmetric noisy voter model has numerous applications, including the description of election dynamics and disease outbreak control. The study's findings highlight the impact of space, arrangement, and symmetry on the model's dynamics and long-term behavior.

This work divides time into two distinct phases in a power-limited device-to-device (D2D) communication scenario that also involves transmitting data and electricity to devices. 
During one time period, a relay transmits data and electricity to end users without external power, and during the other time period, users harness energy from ambient radio waves to decode each other's messages. 
We examine two possible arrangements for these time phases and analyze their effects on overall system performance. 
In one arrangement, the TFIET (Time Switching Based Information and Energy Transfer) method is used, and in the other, an ETIT (Energy Transfer Information Transfer) method is employed. 
To find the ideal delay between these two time periods, we conduct an exhaustive search, and the resulting overall throughput and energy efficiency are compared to those achieved by TFIET and ETIT methods. 
Numerical results show that a significant gain in both throughput and energy efficiency can be attained by finding the optimal delay interval.

Recent telework necessities have led to this author's laboratory being equipped with an extensive array of remote access and automated systems, including the complete automation of a complex experimental system. Consequently, this author has been able to continue conducting experiments despite significant reductions to his laboratory's physical resources. The text that follows presents the details of various remote access and automated system components now in use within the laboratory, along with the programming languages and platforms used for their implementation, as well as the benefits and limitations of each system. Moreover, the programming languages and platforms used for the laboratory's remote access and automated systems are presented as potentially useful to other researchers. Finally, the author expresses the hope that continuing to develop and refine these systems will enable his laboratory to operate successfully into the future.

We present an electron optics package for vector field emitters, known as phase plates, which can reduce the size of electron probes to less than 1 Å with a square arrangement of circular apertures in the center of a square pixel pattern. Although originally intended for scanning transmission electron microscopes, these plates have broader applications in physics and biology that require high-quality electron probes. By utilizing commercial software for electron optics simulation, we determined how factors such as fill-factor, pixel pattern, and electrode geometry affect the electron probe size and current density. Additionally, we measured resistance and temperature distributions in phase plates to prevent thermal deformation during operation.

One-dimensional system harmonic oscillators can maintain their ground state against nonlinear effects, regardless of intensity, when an anharmonic term is included in the Hamiltonian. This study demonstrates that a solitary wave exists that remains stable in this specific model, even with a large anharmonic component, whereas harmonic oscillators with a similar parameter would lose stability. This idealized scenario is meant to highlight that harmonic peaks are not necessarily at the forefront of stable solitary waves in nontraverse systems. Numerical evidence suggests that the solitary wave's profile lies significantly in the harmonic well's anharmonic region.

Let $\mathcal{O}_K$ denote the ring of integers in a number field $K$. This paper tackles the Galois module structure over $\mathcal{O_K}$ for wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of the rational numbers $\Q$. We establish the additive Galois module structure for specific wildly ramified extensions of $\Q$, particularly those with a uniquely determined integral basis invariant under the action of $\text{Gal}(K/\Q)$. Notably, we verify the conjecture by W. Gaschler regarding such structures in the case of a quadratic field with specific discriminant values, namely $p^4$ for a prime number $p$ ranging from $5$ to $19$.

For very short-lived neutral particles, missing energy or momentum signals their disappearance, whereas longer-lived particles require searches tailored to their specific decay lengths. In the case of intermediate lifetime neutral particles, they typically manifest with visible decay tracks, prompting experiments like those at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) to focus on neutral long-lived particles (LLPs) with decay lengths of a few centimeters to a few meters. To this end, researchers have compiled projections for the production of hypothetical scalar muon type scalars with various lifetimes, demonstrating the sensitivity to detect them across different colliders including the Tevatron, the Linear Collider, and the LHC with different detection setups for LLPs.

This paper investigates the causes of distributional semantic changes, focusing on two factors: semantic shifts and changes in contextual variance. Researchers used the Circulo dataset to examine the contextual variability associated with node centers and boundary nodes in a circular layout. Surprisingly, they found that the expected semantic changes resulting from vertex relocation were negligible. However, they did observe a substantial impact of contextual variance on the interpretation of linguistic trends over time. This effect was most pronounced for words with high-dimensional context embeddings and weak for words with high variance. Furthermore, a notable influence of external contexts on node embeddings was revealed, which could be mitigated through a more adaptable graph structure. This research provides a framework for analyzing dynamic representation changes and the effects of context for nodes within a fixed vs. changeable context framework.

We employ the Golovkino observatory data to analyze the sensitivity of the experiment
to various types of ultra-light particles,
including axions, charged axion-like particles, and spin-1 dark matter.
We calculate parameter constraints for the mass of these particles and their
interaction strengths based on the Golovkino observatory data and compare
these to previous results from other experiments.
The findings of this study can be seen in Fig.[[1]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06884)
and Tab.[[2]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.06884).
Assuming the widespread presence of ultra-light particles and assuming that
they constitute dark matter, we can derive a minimum mass threshold for
these particles, which may be compared to other studies in this field.

During retinogenesis, photoreceptor neurons are formed in the outer retina as their nuclei move from the inner retina. Although this process is well-documented, understanding the underlying mechanisms that drive such large-scale migrations remains elusive. By leveraging high-resolution, long-term live imaging of a marker within the mouse outer retina, we observed distinct patterns of nuclear distribution and mobility. Our analysis revealed three distinct phases: an initial period of rapid mixing within the outer retina, followed by a narrowing of the molecular layer and a shift in nuclear behavior, and a final period of sustained organization. Our findings suggest outer retinal nodes play a crucial role in guiding the migration of photoreceptor nuclei, with ensemble-level guidance playing a more significant role than individual identity. By forming a precise template, the migrating population can be efficiently sorted into a perfectly positioned outer retina.

This research focuses on optimizing the mutual coherence of a sensing matrix to enhance the robustness of image reconstruction under the influence of outliers. By integrating the MEster algorithm, which effectively removes outlier effects, with a modified mutual coherence minimization approach, we create a method that minimizes the influence of outliers while improving the compressive sensing performance, all within a single framework. An otSCS framework is proposed, combining these concepts within a single alternative optimization process. The otSCS algorithm iterates on CS and SC parts of the problem, gradually converging to a solution. Numerical experiments on various tasks, including natural and facial image reconstruction from compressed sensing, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, yielding superior results compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

We investigate various active systems across different dimensions (from 2 to 5) 
using the众包 Neumann field-theoretic approach and the functional renormalization 
group method to investigate their critical behavior. 
Our research reveals that these systems exhibit critical dimensions at both the 
microscopic and macroscopic levels, with significant differences in the 
self-similarity exponents compared to other models. 
Additionally, we observe that in dimensions close to the critical level, 
these systems display extensive transitions associated with order parameters, 
while also maintaining storage of memory from initial conditions, 
even after a prolonged duration. 
Furthermore, we find that the transitions change from first-order in 2D 
to continuous in 4D, with corresponding changes in universality classes. 
Our results provide insights into the complex dynamics of active matter across 
different dimensions and can have implications for understanding biological 
systems and other applications.

This paper focuses on a challenging task – extracting personal information from Chinese Resident ID cards, a project with significant value for researchers and organizations studying the Chinese population. To facilitate this research, we have created a high-quality dataset consisting of 2,000 annotated lines of text corresponding to Chinese ID cards, and we have developed a corresponding NLP pipeline to guide accurate text extraction. Our analysis reveals that effective NLP techniques can substantially enhance the accuracy of text extraction from ID cards, with the proposed pipeline achieving an impressive 99.05% accuracy – significantly better than the 94.5% accuracy of the baseline method, with this 5% difference having substantial ramifications in various real-world applications.

Driven quantum systems under periodic driving conditions can be effectively analyzed using time-dependent coherent states, which serve as an optimal representation. We demonstrate this by deriving a precise equation of motion for the periodic driving Heisenberg model. This equation of motion is then used to accurately reproduce the model's properties, which in turn allows for the investigation of entanglement dynamics in both real and frequency spaces.

A study of nine detected exomoons, including a new candidate with three measured orbital periods, aims to understand their physical characteristics. Most exomoons, however, remain enigmatic as they lack information on their shapes, compositions, temperatures, or rotational patterns. A detailed analysis of light curves for nine known exomoons, consisting of nine asteroids with attached moons systems, provides such missing data. Observations revealed that the detected asteroids' rotation was either dormant, spinning in one direction, or had its rate of rotation consistently accelerated. These observations were made at wavelengths between 450 and 900 $	ext{\AA}$.

Let $S$ be a compact surface and let G be the group of homeomorphisms of $S$ that preserve orientation. If a subgroup $\Gamma$ of G acts transitively or solely transitively in a topological sense on the interior of $S$, we demonstrate that this is only possible when the subgroup has a compact or precompact action. Additionally, we show that the group of homeomorphisms of $S$ that are triangular has a closed and precompact action, which implies that a subgroup of such a group has fully trivial invariants when placed within a topological sense.

We investigate the decision problem for rational function continuity, specifically at a given point in R^n, and prove that it is logarithmic-depth reducible from TQFT and vice versa, establishing TQFT's inclusion within the first level of the logarithmic-depth hierarchy, including constant-factor logarithmic-depth inclusion both directions. Moreover, we set a lower-bound for rational function continuity, showing it is non-trivially reducible from a specific segment of the logarithmic-depth hierarchy.

This study utilizes a complex system, characterized by disparate time scales and large-amplitude dynamics coexisting, to evaluate a reservoir computing approach called echo state recurrence predictor. Although traditional models, such as phase spaces with co-existing attractors separated by unstable manifolds, feature disparate time scales on either side, our analysis focuses on a Lorenz-96 model with a reservoir predictor. By training and testing the model on different co-existing phase spaces, we demonstrate the ability to handle simultaneous competition between different dynamics. With a small time scale gap and near-by distribution of phase spaces, the system exhibits transient behavior before switching to a specific attractor. However, as the time scale gap increases, the system requires a significantly larger reservoir to accurately predict the slow dynamics after the transition. Ultimately, our study reveals the challenges in predicting transient dynamics and the limitations in handling disparate time scales and co-existing phase spaces.

Feedback control systems rely on state-computable reachable state sets to ensure reliable performance. Our novel approach demonstrates that reliable, robust systems can be designed for non-deterministic plants with simple state holders that meet a specified time constraint. Our approach also reveals that robust systems can be designed for deterministic plants with minimal state holders that meet the same constraint. For non-deterministic plants, we can compute the set of reachable states and then derive a reachable quotient by feedback laws, allowing us to find reachable states within the time constraint. For deterministic plants, we can compute the quotient by feedback laws from the set of reachable states, allowing us to identify the set of states that can be reached within the time constraint. In both cases, the difference between the computed set of reachable states and the actual state space is finite. If the set of reachable states is regular, the system can be determined with a finite state holder, and the quotient by feedback laws can be computed to find the set of states that can be managed within the time constraint. In summary, our mathematical framework provides a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between deterministic and non-deterministic plants, and the role of feedback control in computing reachable state sets and designing robust systems.

People's beliefs in the existence of independent objects within the animacy spectrum are a key factor in language acquisition and usage. To investigate the underlying assumptions of the general population, we conducted two large-scale online experiments, each enrolling over 500 participants. In these experiments, readers were presented with short, ambiguous passages and asked to determine whether the ambiguous entities within them were of indeterminable, non-living, or living nature. Our results revealed that readers' interpretations of these entities' existence as independent agents or categorizable objects of the non-living world were both significantly correlated with perceived animacy. Notably, understanding of the scene itself had no impact on perceived animacy. Furthermore, we found that entities deemed as independent were significantly more likely to be perceived as living, whereas categorizable objects of the non-living world were more frequently interpreted as of animal nature. This distinct relationship between the two was less clear when entities were of indeterminable nature. Our findings suggest that both visual categorizability and agency are of separate significance in perceiving the existence of independent entities within the animacy continuum.

Lev Landau and Claude Singer once posed an unsolved problem in mathematics, posing a fascinating hypothesis regarding the distribution of zeros in automorphic L-functions. Specifically, they suggested that the minimal distance between any two zeros in such L-functions is directly influenced by the degree of symmetry in the associated automorphic form. In contrast, most researchers believe this problem has no solution, arguing that zero repulsion shouldn't occur due to the wide distribution of zeros across different instances. However, this assumption may be incorrect, as instances with dense zero clusters appear to be increasingly rare with distance measuring in powers of two, as opposed to an expected uniform distribution measuring in powers of q. Although numerical evidence isn't sufficient for a proof, it does suggest the influence of classical obstacles, once considered irrelevant, from both singulo-real and pseudo-real scenarios. To address this problem, we discovered an influence that grows quadratically in the conductor, as measured in steps of two, initially inspired by the conjectured impact of singular zeros, which some believe don't truly repel each other. This discovery is directly related to the existence of Landau-Siegel zeros, and in the process, we found an affirmative answer to Singer's question, stating that the minimal distance between any two zeros in the set of L-functions associated to a family of 2-level symmetric compact modular forms is consistently bounded from below.

Quantitative input-output behavior is a crucial concept for understanding robust algorithms, membership verification, and resistant quantum computing. Building upon these ideas, we develop a novel quantum logical framework, inspired by Trix's work, that provides safe guidelines for constructing quantum programs with a quantitative input-output perspective. Our logic allows for precise measurement of a quantum program's responses to both quantum and classical inputs, outputting only classical data. We prove that our logic is consistent and equips it with a reliable method of verifying the behavior of existing and future quantum algorithms. In practice, we apply our logic to analyze the robust median-finding algorithm from Moerdiak et al., as well as a quantum variant of the rounding algorithm from Shpilka and禹, representing the median as a range. Our approach also yields a quantitative version of the range theorem of Algorithm 2 from Moerdiak et al. Additionally, we establish a quantitative version of the bank rounding relationship from Regev and Smith, and investigate the algorithm from Shpilka and禹 through our logical framework.

In detailed calculations based on an enclosed room model, various factors such as infection duration, virus transmissibility, and population size are considered to estimate the number of potential super-spreader events. A key finding from this study is that in densely populated groups, most infections are caused by super-spreader events, which significantly impact the epidemic's growth rate and overall dynamics. To account for this, a standard epidemiological model is modified to match the results of the room model, showing that it can accurately predict the time-dependent growth of infections when a population is large enough. Furthermore, the time it takes for the number of infections to double can be estimated using this growth rate, which is observed to be as long as 4.5 days in a highly contagious scenario, providing a window of opportunity to contain an outbreak before it spreads to a broader population.

We introduce the notion of a codiskcyclic $C_0$-semigroup of operators, which specifically refers to codiskcyclic semigroups that possess a uniform codiskcyclicity property. Subsequent sections provide examples of codiskcyclic $C_0$-semigroups and explore the relationship between codiskcyclicity and cyclicity, demonstrating that every cyclical semigroup is either cyclical or codiskcyclic.

Accurate estimation of infrared star formation rates is affected by reliable maps of magnetic fields. Magnetic field measurements using the SOHO/MDI instrument's Sine-Greenstein method can be distorted by inaccuracies in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in regions of weak fields and high inclination angles. A novel approach corrects these issues by adjusting for magnetic fill fraction and is demonstrated using a high-resolution field from the $\eta$ Per cluster at 160 parsecs, yielding a model of the intrinsic magnetic field structure. This adjusted method when applied to the $\eta$ Per cluster and another high-resolution field, results in inverted magnetic field distributions that no longer falsely suggest random magnetic field patterns in spiral arm regions. This corrected approach can be effectively applied to other young stellar objects to produce improved external magnetic field maps, thus aiding in the creation of more accurate magnetic field distributions and enhancing our understanding of star formation processes.

We introduce an innovative variance reduction technique for Monte Carlo simulations, utilizing complex-valued affine coupling layers to modify the random walk path. This method reduces the variance of the estimator without affecting its accuracy, and our empirical evidence indicates that it outperforms existing variance reduction techniques, especially when estimating paths of moderate to high complexity. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that it is feasible to incorporate complex values into the neural network components of the control variates framework, achieving significant variance reduction with minimal computational cost.

Given a subshift $X$ and its associated topological entropy $h(X)$, the topological entropy of the subshift $X'$ produced by applying a recognizable morphism $\sigma$ is bounded, specifically $h(X') \leq \sigma$ to $h(X)$. This research also delves into the conditions where the topological entropy remains unchanged, i.e., when $h(X') = \sigma$ to $h(X)$, and explores the implications on the alphabet size when this equality holds.

Utilizing pre-trained language models in unsupervised tasks like word-sentence editing has seen a rise in effectiveness, with a key technique being the integration of external knowledge, such as knowledge graphs, to improve the performance of these models. Building on this foundation, a novel approach called ReCross is proposed, which mimics the KGCIN method's fine-tuning process in a initial stage, and in a subsequent stage, employs a refined version of the ReCross method that utilizes the original knowledge and corresponding sentences, allowing the model to absorb this information and master the editing task simultaneously. A significant aspect of the proposed method involves a multi-task setup with a contrastive loss that extracts additional information from the knowledge graph and translates it into a human-comprehensible format. Experimental results using a state-of-the-art model called T5 demonstrate that the ReCross method achieves the most efficient performance across both single-stage and two-stage configurations, surpassing the original approach by a notable margin.

Process tuning is a crucial step in achieving excellent performance for many machine learning tasks, including HPC workflow optimization. Nevertheless, exploring options through conventional evaluation methods like grid search can be deemed inappropriate when dealing with sensitive data in processes like workflows. For instance, training a model on private data and then sharing it also constitutes a form of information exchange. To overcome this limitation, this paper introduces a novel framework for efficient and optimal hyperparameter exploration that enhances the efficiency and accounts for the interactions between dataset sizes and parameters, while ensuring that private information remains secure. This design is feasible and allows for the retrieval of a model, which can be used to assess its performance. Additionally, the framework's ability to efficiently use time is demonstrated, including an example of acquiring a proxy with 50 times less expense than the original task, while maintaining the accuracy of the results.

We have established that the spherical wedge numbers, denoted as $sw_n(W)$, for a Coxeter group $W$, form an ascending sequence that indicates the minimum number of spheres in a contractible sphere-wedged configuration for $W_n$, particularly within a specific subsymmetry type. Additionally, these numbers are found to be identical to those proposed by Casson and Blecher, provided the Coxeter group is finite.

We developed a technique for accurately determining chemically abnormal stars' plasma temperatures by using their residual element abundance patterns, which reflect similar underlying stellar population characteristics. This method was applied to two star groups, the HIP 69409 family and HD 168426 family, which exhibit lithium richness. By comparing the residual patterns of these families to those of a control group of normal lithium-depleted, metal-poor stars, we identified consistent element abundance features, particularly in the titanium group. This discovery suggests that these particular elements are affected by similar processes affecting low-core temperature, metal-poor stars. Furthermore, by examining the magnitude of residual patterns, we determined that the hip 69409 and HD 168426 families display identical distribution ranges as the metal-poor, lithium-drashting stellar population, which implies that these two families share the same historical evolution path. This study demonstrates that by analyzing stellar element abundance patterns, we can gain valuable insights into the most drashtic and well-drashtic stars and stellar groups, potentially linking stars that appear unrelated at their surfaces to a common origin.

This paper utilizes a dynamic attenuation model based on network analysis to examine the influence of precursor events and geographical information on a specific type of geographic-aware information cascade decay. Through simulation experiments, we discover that pre-occuring events at a location can extend the range of cascade decay attenuation, whereas the effect of geographic information cascade decay can vary, either increasing or decreasing its intensity. Further investigations into the interaction between multiple cascade topics reveal that they can either share information or compete for attention. Ultimately, our research provides novel insights and theoretical explanations for geographic-aware cascade dynamics, and can have valuable applications in promoting public health safety, managing emergency responses, and guiding advertising strategies.

We have examined over 6,000 nebulae in the Fornax cluster using the VCC database,
filtering out those with significant errors in nebular flux to focus on a representative
sample for analyzing the PNF. A revised version of the NFW calculation was performed
using our specific sub-sample of the PNF from the Fornax cluster. To further validate
our findings, we compared the NFW results with those obtained through other methods,
which showed a general consistency within approximately 10%.
Our calculated distance to the Fornax cluster was around 19.66 Mpc.
The NFW also yielded the cluster's velocity dispersion,
which indicated the need for a higher PNF sampling in brighter nebulae beyond magnitude -3.54,
as well as a possible influence from local structure, dark matter sub-halo effects,
or a potential variation in gravitational constant within the cluster.

Recent advancements in vector instruction sets have fueled the development of high-performance numerical libraries, yet questions remain about their transferability to real-world data. To investigate this issue, we created LifeStream, an open-source, scalable framework designed for iterative algorithms utilizing vector instructions, and which manages diverse data types and distributions. Performance evaluations show LifeStream outperforms equivalent hand-optimized libraries when working on most real-world datasets, and scales effectively across multiple processors.

This research paper focuses on extending the concept of Bertrand curves from 2+1 dimensional Minkowski space to 3+1 dimensional Minkowski space, specifically for both rectangular and lightlike (rogue) systems. We derive the conditions necessary for a curve to be considered a Bertrand curve in each of these spaces.

For nearly five decades, deep neural underrepresentation has plagued the field, with many straightforward tasks suffering from a lack of effective solutions. This includes simple yet impactful problems like KL Divergence, Click Through Rate, and Logits Mahalanobis Distance, which have seen a significant decline in performance. We have been unable to compare these methods fairly due to the need for hyperparameter tuning, data leakage, and incorrect gradient computation. To address this challenge, we present a standardized and corrected baseline for these tasks, with the help of an extensive framework that will enable future research to build upon. We have retrained the same network architecture on the CTR task using the new, fixed baseline, and were surprised to see a 4% drop in performance compared to the commonly used Binary Cross Entropy loss function. This research will continue with the hope of discovering more efficient and effective deep learning methods.

Many products and biological structures rely on polymer materials, which undergo significant stiffening during strain-induced crystallization. To design products with optimized mechanical properties, a comprehensive understanding of the SC process at both micro and macro levels is necessary. Based on a analysis of existing literature, we present a new general framework for modeling the thermomechanical process of SC, utilizing powerful objective principles such as material objectivity, balance laws, local objectivity, and the thermodynamic potential maximum principle. This approach leads to a proposal of an energy-based, phenoменological constitutive model for the SC process, which accounts for partial ordering induced by bond realignment and recombination, and results in a constitutive equation for the stress tensor and an additional heat source term in the energy equation. This heat source term, which plays a crucial role in accurately predicting the temperature field, is directly related to the induced partial order and the degree of local orientation. Demonstrating the proposed model's capability, we simulate the scattering of thermal filaments in the wake of a moving blade, which represents the fundamental mechanism of SC.

Our calculation of magnetic susceptibility is based on a first-principles approach, considering classical and quantum contributions, and uses a method that preserves the accuracy of density functional theory, especially for systems with large unit cells. We determine susceptibility across two and three-dimensional space, and our results match closely with existing data obtained through experimental and traditional methods. Verifying the validity of our approach, we find that the topology of a system's Fermi surface significantly influences the pattern of magnetic susceptibility, which is confirmed through a case study on body-centered copper.

This research focuses on enhancing error rates in CPM signal detection using conventional differential detection methods. Initially, we establish a higher bound than the existing conventional SPD bound for minimum symbol error rates. Furthermore, we propose an improved differential detection method that outperforms the conventional approach, particularly when the spectral shape factor is large. Our analysis shows that the proposed detector's performance depends on whether a specific inequality involving the spectral shape factor and symbol rate holds true, with error rates varying accordingly. Ultimately, we observe that, given a specific maximum symbol error rate and differential phase constraint, our detector can achieve better results with a larger spectral shape factor, surpassing the conventional detector's capabilities.

We demonstrate that the close match between grand canonical and canonical ensembles for systems with a sufficiently small compressibility can also apply to systems where the grand canonical ensemble is typically not appropriate, specifically those exhibiting large volumes to surface area ratios. The validity of using the grand canonical ensemble as an approximation for the canonical one depends on the system's volume, regardless of its ensemble approach. Our analysis highlights the limitations of employing the grand canonical ensemble to calculate extensive properties, such as chemical potential, which directly impacts the accuracy of predicting phenomena like phase transitions in systems where the volume is not an appropriate extensive parameter.

To enable automated discovery of rules in natural language, we investigated the barriers preventing a seamless integration of semantic representations and rules. Our research indicates that the linear organization of many rule formats, such as if-then relations, creates obstacles to this integration. We observed that networks struggle to distinguish between semantically identical statements when presented with varied rule formats. Furthermore, we found that providing a hierarchical understanding of rule types facilitates the distinction between statements and predicts the initial difficulty in recognizing patterns behind explicit rules. Our findings are derived from multiple experimental analyses using a diverse set of math problems with clear if-then structures, and our data suggests that addressing format obstacles is a crucial step towards building a coherent model of reasoning based solely on explicit rules.

Our analysis focuses on a specific implementation of the NISQ-HHL algorithm, which incorporates an improved dynamic frequency encoding method to avoid the Hamiltonian simulation step in the HHL algorithm's quantum circuit. We evaluated a particular instance of this NISQ-HHL algorithm, known as the "zero" variant, which omits the Hamiltonian simulation step entirely. Our study involved creating a simplified model to represent the fidelity losses encountered during various quantum gate operations and determined the feasible precision achievable when applying the "zero" variant to find solutions to linear systems of equations. Our findings reveal that the NISQ-HHL algorithm can achieve a 10^-3 precision when solving the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in a limited regime, which could enable the scientific community to begin leveraging these findings and accelerate the algorithm development process.

We introduce a novel method for integrating linguistic and speech information in automated speech recognition systems, specifically our BiAM, or bidirectional attention mechanism, to model the complex relationship between these two domains. By employing attention models in both forward and reverse directions, we capture the asymmetrical nature of this relationship, which allows for detailed analysis of its inherent properties. Our experiments on the Librispeech test set using our BiAM achieve a word error rate of 4.9%, which represents a significant improvement over the current state-of-the-art rates. Furthermore, this research provides a further examination of our BiAM's capacity to leverage pre-existing knowledge, which offers valuable insights for enhancing the performance of ASR systems with low-resource datasets.

We delve into the effects of node deletions on Moshers' parking distributions by examining the consequence of removing a randomly selected node. As $n$, the size of the initial structure, approaches infinity, the total and Kolmogorov distances both expand at a rate of $\sqrt{n}$. To counterbalance this growth, we consider a sequence of $n$-sized structures, where the difference in distance between two structures of size $n$ and $n+1$ is less than $1/\sqrt{n}$. Both conditions, together, contribute to establishing bounds on the derivative of the parking distribution's measure with respect to the uniform distribution, which is shown to be bounded by a constant. Ultimately, these findings are summarized as $(n)$.

We employ a dual representation consisting of a language label and its corresponding novel-view video target to enhance the task of predicting videos from different viewpoints within a semantic space. By using a fixed label-to-view transformation model, we can predict videos from different viewpoints for objects that have been seen before. A neural dynamic model is used to predict the changes required to obtain videos for new objects. This allows us to leverage large-scale pretraining and effectively reduce the novel-view prediction task to learning label-to-view transformations for known objects and dynamics for new objects. Experiments conducted on multiple datasets including real and synthetic objects show that this approach successfully generates coherent and view-consistent videos for both novel views and new objects.

We experimentally create entanglement between photonic higher-order modes and apply this concept to build a phase beam-splitter device. By using curved photonic waveguides, we generate specific higher-order modes, and then an asymmetric beam splitter facilitates interaction between these modes, resulting in a Faraday effect. We demonstrate a unique state of light with horizontal and vertical polarization components that are in a coherent superposition and linked by the Faraday rotation. This distinct state of light is detected via direct measurement. Our research presents a straightforward experimental method to create and measure circular polarization entanglement involving higher-order photonic modes.

Using an effective relativistic three-body Hamiltonian that incorporates the spin, orbital angular angularulation, tensor forces, and spin-orbit forces, we derive and classify resonance mass spectra for $B_{cc}^{++}$, $B_{cs}^{0}$, and $\Xi_{cc}^{+}$ baryons in the charmonium-baryon and strange-meson-baryon systems. A key component of our calculation is the evaluation of two-body potentials within the mass spectra analysis. Our computations yield precise results for both ground and excited states, yielding predicted masses, widths, quantum numbers, and their corresponding probabilities for $B_{cc}^{++}$, $B_{cs}^{0}$, and $\Xi_{cc}^{+}$ baryons.

A mathematical well-mixed model is developed to predict aerosol concentration near an infected person within a small enclosed space, considering factors like breathing rates, exhaled aerosol sizes, air recirculation, and room characteristics. It also incorporates a geometric approach to determine how different room shapes affect aerosol distribution. Despite its simplicity, the model accurately forecasts aerosol concentrations for various scenarios and is capable of generalizing to more complex room configurations. Its efficacy is demonstrated through simulations that match measured data from experiments and are applicable to predicting aerosol concentration in rooms with multiple infected individuals.

We investigated the DC Hall effect in 5nm Co layers surrounded by varying numbers of 5nm Bi layers in Cubano multilayers, and found that in single and double Co/Bi layers, the Hall effect is dominated by the bulk contribution from Co. However, in multilayers with five or more Bi layers, scattering from the Bi layers becomes the primary factor influencing the Hall effect, switching from interface to interlayer scattering. This change was reflected in the slope of R_{HH} vs t_{Co} and R_{SH} vs t_{Co} plots, which did not account for the thickness of the first Co layer. The shift from interface to interlayer effects was confirmed by the recovery of R_{SH} vs t_{Co} plot slope, which matched the Hall resistance of Polycrystalline Co.

We have derived an lower bound for the fractional N-dimensional Schrödinger equations with $1/\alpha$ potential to clarify how the $\alpha$ parameter impacts impact as $\alpha$ moves towards 1 and $N$ dimensions.

A previously unexplored issue in safety-critical machine learning concerns selecting a risk measurement method that guarantees neural network safety while maintaining efficient performance. We formulated a neural network training problem with restrictions, suitable for use in safety-critical applications and demonstrated how varying $p$-norms impact the optimal solution. A previously unexamined solution for a specific constraint, involving a neural network trained with a maximum entropy loss, is a key finding of our research. Our evidence suggests that a diverse set of approaches, including training a generic self-supervised learning model, can be understood through the lens of our proposed framework. This includes showing that such approaches are equivalent to training a specific type of neural network with a maximum entropy loss and a bounded Lipschitz constant. Our findings have broader implications, as they can be applied to improve the safety and efficiency of machine learning models in various contexts.

Vector leptoquark searches in top-quark final states could further be optimized by implementing a new method for background estimation, specifically for T+jets searches with two top-quarks. Initially, the author found that NLO precise background predictions, particularly for colored particles like vector leptoquarks, yielded substantially tighter constraints compared to current ATLAS constraints in their T+dijet searches. Moreover, the author's analysis of current experiments indicates that achieving expected sensitivity in the forthcoming Run~3 could be surpassed by utilizing a new background estimation method for single-top processes, specifically for the 0-jet and 1-jet categories, which predominantly contain vector leptoquark signal-like characteristics.

Although deep learning has made significant progress in low-dose PET image reconstruction, using it for very low-dose PET reconstructions remains challenging due to the incorporation of pronounced statistical noise. In this study, we present a novel deep-neural-network (DNN) framework that combines a trained non-linear operator with a coherent speckle pattern to produce high-quality PET images, even in low-dose scenarios. To account for the high level of random noise present in low-dose PET data, we developed a new variance estimation module that dynamically varies the intensity of the coherent speckle pattern. Evaluations using both synthetic and clinical data demonstrated that this proposed method yields notable improvements in image quality when compared to several state-of-the-art DNN-based reconstruction techniques, particularly in cases with higher noise levels. Moreover, this proposed framework allows users to control the level of structural detail in the reconstructed images by adjusting a single parameter.

Neural coreference resolution models have reached a level of understanding that allows for examining complex linguistic theories, such as centering theory. Prior studies on this have however relied on simplified versions of the theory, leaving out an analysis of how contextualized embeddings affect the performance in relation to the more comprehensive theory. This study has thus far as it fills this gap by evaluating a neural coreference resolution model based on the full RCTT. Furthermore, it examines the effectiveness of current coreference resolution methods across the performance spectrum and finds that contextualized embeddings neither substantially nor consistently enhance the results.

WiFi localization technology has seen rapid development in recent years, particularly in how
location estimation is done. Machine learning methods have surpassed traditional approaches in
precision for estimating ground-to-air distance using WiFi signals. However, deploying these
machine learning models at a large scale for predicting distances between GPS coordinates is
challenging due to their reliance on data labeling. In a search-based framework that
combines machine learning with graph-based fingerprint organization, this paper presents a
novel, flexible graph-embedding method to efficiently predict distances between GPS coordinates
using only binary data from access points. To achieve this prediction with limited labeled
information, this method uses the binary data to determine the relative position of each
fingerprint, which is then used to build a minimum spanning tree (MST) that connects
similar fingerprints. A machine learning model is trained to predict the distances between

This research paper examines how different beam patterns affect beam interactions with multiple-pass energy-saving systems and determines the minimum energy current that can be safely handled. A custom-made code was created to calculate the position and velocity of particles within each RF bucket across different treatment lengths, providing a way to analyze and visualize the effects of various treatment patterns on the overall efficiency and effectiveness of therapy. Our examinations of four different pattern-options revealed that selecting an optimal pattern can significantly reduce the beam-interaction effects and increase the threshold current that can be safely handled. A key finding was that certain patterns could delay the onset of beam-interaction effects and allow for a larger number of stages in an energy-saving linac. Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights into how to design and optimize multi-stage energy-saving linacs that are both efficient and effective in delivering cancer therapy.

We calculate the leading logarithmic two-glue scalar conformal entropy value for this physical state within the 't Hooft limit of 't Hooft Yang-Mills theory and find a direct connection to the four-gluon amplitude within $	ext{N=4}$ super Yang-Mills theory, yielding a specific value of $28	au_1	tau_2$ amplitude.

The flat-surface brush theory is highly effective, yet it breaks down at the interface of spherical surfaces with varying curvature. A new dimensional analysis has been developed to examine polymer brushes on curved surfaces and determine when the standard flat-surface model no longer applies. On convex surfaces, increased surface curvature leads to a additional free energy cost during stretching, prompting an investigation into the impact of surface geometry on brush properties. Conversely, on concave surfaces, polymer brushes exhibit decreased dimensional density due to the divergent area. Both phenomena result in altered solvent interactions and swelling patterns, leading to displaced profile boundaries and changes in polymer chain dimension. The analysis also considers the effect of grafted polymer chain length and surface curvature, demonstrating that decreased density on concave surfaces can cause unexpected changes in brush properties, including a shift in polymer chain conformation.

When we modify a graph's metric dimension by adjusting geodesic distances beyond a certain point, a new dimension known as the truncated metric dimension arises. For a truncated distance of one, the dimension returns to the traditional metric dimension. As the distance threshold increases, the dimension generally decreases or stays the same. The article proves a gap exists for graphs with truncated metric dimension gaps of two, specifically showing that some graphs with an infinite dimension have subgraphs with a truncated metric dimension of two. Additionally, an formula is derived that relates the truncated metric dimension to the graph's maximum degree and the threshold value.

An in-depth examination of the luminosity variability in AGN is made possible through extensive, multi-year observations, as demonstrated by recent studies. However, an inevitable byproduct of observation technology introduces a significant challenge when analyzing long-term variability patterns – namely, the inevitable hourly time-scale effects of atmospheric and telescopic influences known as "reddening" and "magnification." A unique and extensive dataset, consisting of 10,000 hours of Hubble Space Telescope observations of the AGN M87, presented an ideal opportunity to develop a robust method for distinguishing between true variability patterns and instrumental artifacts. By creating a model based on color-magnitude relationships, we were able to effectively separate the intrinsic variability patterns from the external effects of space telescopes.

A well-known result by Shapley and Shubik established that the optimal social welfare in a simple market model is bounded, specifically within a factor of 1/√n from the maximum possible welfare for a market where participants can trade discrete units of different goods. Since this initial breakthrough, research into this market model has expanded significantly, influenced heavily by its application to bandwidth allocation in communication networks. A key assumption made by most studies on this model, however, is that methods of measuring value are based on fundamental principles, reflecting an objective reality. In stark contrast, a new, provocative theory proposed in this paper suggests that valuation methods may be far more subjective, influenced by psychological and strategic considerations, and may not always adhere to basic axiomatic principles. In particular, new, innovative models of flexibility in measuring value are introduced that challenge the traditional perspective, demonstrating how even the most benign, straightforward methods of valuation can lead to substantial deviations from the ideal, underlying objective values. As a result, even a basic exchange market algorithm is shown to potentially approximate welfare within a reasonable range, specifically between 1/p maximum and p times the maximum for a factor p > 1, while, in contrast, more complex, non-trivial models of valuation are shown to yield larger, potentially unbounded deviation from the maximum possible welfare.

This research paper performs binary asteroid candidate identification using data from the ATLAS wide-field survey, processed through an adapted version of the point spread function analysis method. With a sampling rate of approximately 15 minutes and a detection limit of 22 magnitudes, the analysis focuses on binary asteroid candidates by examining the temporal and spatial characteristics of detected objects. A sample of N=24 objects, potentially including binary asteroids, was obtained. Furthermore, formulae for calculating the uncertainty of the binary companion's position relative to the main body were provided, which is useful in distinguishing binary asteroids from other objects, such as stellar objects with apparent motion, occultation events, and colliding asteroids.

Recent studies in economics have highlighted the significance of peer influence within networks. Yet, estimating this phenomenon remains challenging due to the lack of exogenous variation in network structures and the difficulty in obtaining comprehensive data on networks and associated variables. This research proposes utilizing the random assignment of access to a digital good on a specific platform to generate the necessary exogenous variation in networks, which, when combined with the assignment data, allows for the estimation of peer influence through both theoretical and empirical approaches. By doing so, the method leverages the ease with which digital goods assignments can be treated as a proxy for networks, facilitating more accurate influence estimates. Moreover, the estimates derived from this approach are directly comparable to traditional methods that rely on in-depth platform data and extensive variable sets.

Seven chain rule formulas for fractional operators of variable order are presented in this research, combining approaches from two established works. Both initial chain rule formulas of variable order rely on absolutely continuous functions of the fractional integral, while three additional formulas of variable order are developed that do not require this condition, utilizing the orthogonal representation of these integrals instead. Both methods ultimately yield equivalent results for non-singular fractional operators of variable order, but apply to different ranges of values.

Collaborative games involving multiple agents can greatly benefit from effective cooperation, which in turn depends on a partner's theory-of-mind (ToM) capabilities. Prior research has utilized human-in-the-loop methods to enhance ToM for simple, single-goal games with visible thinking processes. However these studies have not accounted for multiple concurrent objectives typical of real-world scenarios. We conducted two experiments using a simultaneous multi-goal application called 'Memory', leveraging invisible thinking processes using a heuristic approach. Results show that a ToM approach significantly improves goal achievement probability, particularly when concurrent objectives vary widely across all possible quadrants of a 2D space, even when a significant level of interference is present.

We investigated how topological defects in shallow and deeply knotted proteins influence their folding processes. Using a coarse-grained model, we found that these proteins exhibit distinct dynamics: folding starts with a nucleation of a folded loop, followed by the incorporation of a loose end into this loop. In contrast, deeply knotted proteins undergo an intermediate step where a tight loop forms by drawing the loose end close to the nucleation site. This loop then engages in a search for the loose end to complete the knot. These findings are supported by empirical evidence and can be applied to understand the folding mechanisms of complex proteins.

Given any closed symplectic manifold, one can find infinitely many nearly symplectic structures that are not equivalent symplectically. A key requirement in the definition of these structures is a topological nature, specifically that the application of the symplectic form is non-degenerate. Notably, this condition can be altered provided the resulting form remains within the same cohomology class.

In the context of a massive dark matter-nucleus system, a new type of interaction is postulated through the creation of a massive Nambu-Goldstone boson. To provide a framework for this, a kaon condensation-like model has been modelled with a complex scalar field representing the dark matter and another representing the nucleus. However, an analysis of a mass term coupling these two fields reveals a discrepancy with the proposed scenario. Consequently, an alternative method to achieve the desired mass term is explored through the coupling of the two fields to a dark U(1) gauge field, leading to a non-abelian version of the model. Furthermore, the possible scenario where the mass term arises from the decay of a heavy field in the potential is also examined. Next, the non-abelian model is applied to the formation of a new phase, a "dark kaon" or "pion" condensation. The resulting dynamics of the model are also examined through the generation of the mass term through the decay of the heavy field. Additionally, the possible implications of the model for the abundance of dark matter and the characteristics of the cosmic microwave background are discussed.

Researchers are using model-based training to reduce the amount of real training needed and make systems more reliable. Using training datasets generated by AI models that adhere to their physical constraints, it has been demonstrated multiple times that robust and flexible machine learning is possible. Despite these promising results, using these methods effectively in realistic scenarios remains difficult, primarily because the systems' stability across different devices is limited and they are easily disrupted by sudden changes. To overcome these challenges, this study enhances training robustity significantly by combining this approach with a model-based training method, which is done successfully with another variational model-based training, resulting in much greater systems' stability and robustness, particularly when a machine learning model is retrained in a new environment.

High-quality epitaxial silicon is prepared using a resistive heating method on a graphene-coated copper substrate at a growth temperature between 1150 and 1300 Celsius. A study reveals that higher temperatures favor the (005) domain, while lower temperatures promote the (111) domain formation. Unexpectedly, reducing temperatures below 1200 Celsius results in a significant increase in grain size. Large-area epitaxial silicon with a minimum thickness of 95 nm and a minimum mobility of 850 cm V-1 s-1 is achieved. Moreover, by leveraging the varying domain preferences, a method that allows for patterned domain selection across large samples is developed.

We introduce a novel method to reduce the rank bound for $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes through the use of modular reduction, building upon a technique initially proposed in [36]. This approach provides an enhanced tool in code construction and allows for an in-depth examination of reduced rank bounds for $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes. We derive an interval of possible ranks for these codes, which is bounded by two functions of code length, and demonstrate various applications of the reduced rank bounds in evaluating equivalent $ \mathbb{Z}_3 \oplus \mathbb{Z}_9 $-linear codes and Cayley graphs. We calculate and compare the bounds on code ranks, including those related to Cayley graphs, and calculate the exact ranks for several specific codes and their associated Cayley graphs.

Annotation cost reduction is crucial for large-scale multi-task learning. However, creating single-to-multi-label correspondence requires careful consideration. This research introduces the single to multiple labels sampling method, allowing an expert to sample a label from the distribution of possible labels given a specific single label. This is beneficial because any label that can be easily included in a sample can be considered important for a model to learn. This research shows the S2M sampling method's advantage by formulating the problem as a ideal utility maximization and using the auxiliary multi-task learning to approximate it. This approach allows the S2M sampled data to be effectively used in various applications, including label completion and applications. Evaluations on 10 existing S2M sampling methods and three new baselines indicate that the S2M data can be employed to build an effective multi-task learning model. The method's effectiveness is particularly evident in scenarios where labels are missing.

Given any category that is wired, we prove that the assignment of fibers forms a functor whose precise parameters can be estimated. If the original category is doubly wired, we show that this functor's behavior is universally determined. We also establish that certain identities and equations hold in the wired version of the construction that assigns these fibers, and that this wired construction satisfies a form of weak naturality.

We employed an advanced model that incorporates magnetic field dynamics, electron heating, and synchrotron self-absorption to interpret the mid- and late-stage radio emissions from the blast wave, specifically for the subshock MAD model. Using this framework, we analyzed 14 blazar cases with well-documented spectral energy distributions from MeV to GeV gamma-rays. We found that the model successfully produces GeV gamma-rays without additional assumptions, and can interpret most gamma-ray bursts observed recently. We also determined that the electron heating rate must fall between $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-2}$ to explain the observed GeV gamma-rays, and this range holds significant implications for Subshock MAD theories. We discovered that the MAD model allows up to 10% of the dyadic power to be emitted as gamma-rays, while optical photons account for less than 1%.

A major challenge in using phonetic stress patterns for detecting cardiac abnormalities is the susceptibility of this approach to noise interference. To address this issue, a novel method has been proposed that employs auto-encoders to effectively reduce speech noise. This technique is seamlessly integrated into a phonetic stress-based classifier for detecting arrhythmias, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through extensive testing on the widely-used HITEEEE dataset, which includes both healthy and abnormal heart rhythms, including bigeminy, trigeminy, and escape beats. Experimental results indicate that the proposed system is capable of accurately classifying cardiac rhythms with escape beats and provides a satisfactory level of accuracy in detecting signals containing cardiac abnormalities even in noisy environments.

A major obstacle in developing intelligent health care systems is created by secure and private data dissemination. To overcome this challenge, we present FedHealth, an innovative wearable activity recognition framework based on Federated Learning. FedHealth enables multiple users to train a shared model without exchanging their data by adapting the selection of update frequencies to individual devices and employing an attention mechanism that boosts the accuracy of activity recognition. Experimental results on public datasets demonstrate the superior accuracy of FedHealth in comparison to conventional methods and confirm its versatility in addressing various activity recognition tasks on wearable devices.

This paper addresses critical factors in investment portfolio strategy development, emphasizing the significance of optimization methodologies employed. Various optimization methodologies are compared, with references to existing research studies. Additionally, alternative interpretations and perspectives on current portfolio assessment metrics, such as Value at Risk and Sharpe Ratio, are explored. Existing studies linking these metrics to more fundamental principles are also examined. Ultimately, the relationship between these concepts and their implications for effective portfolio strategy development are discussed. A summary of key findings is presented, along with suggestions for future research and developments.

This work explores how to incorporate natural language into the interview arrangement and assessment panel organization processes for a given set of candidates within a short time frame.
This problem can be seen as an integrated version of multiple optimization tasks, featuring distinct components with differing magnitudes.
It includes arranging interviews for candidates who can be accommodated within available time slots, selecting the most effective panel from multiple options, and choosing an optimal evaluation function from various alternatives, all with differing levels of complexity.
Furthermore, constraints related to panel selection and evaluation functions impact the arrangement of interviews, introducing additional interdependencies.
We develop a straightforward yet effective approach based on re-formulating the issue, and present a natural language-based framework for conducting recruitment through an example using the COIRec system.
This framework utilizes a combination of a parameterized decision circuit and custom Python scripts for automated analysis.
It also includes a language that expresses the recruitment requirements, which can be interpreted by the system to generate the most effective plan within given constraints, and it is demonstrated with actual data to showcase its practical application.

This research focuses on a novel game theory problem involving a finite time horizon, where a limited patient gamer seeks to maximize a payoff that depends on whether a more patient opponent has completed a specific task. The underlying task is represented by a stochastic differential equation, and the more patient controller can influence the payoff by deciding if the equation includes the controller's diffusion component. The underlying inclusion of this influence is reflected in the optimal decision to include or exclude the diffusion component. The main result of this study, Lemma 5.2, establishes the non-existence of optimal solutions to the equation in the case where the underlying parameter is not equal to the target value. The proofs for both the existence and non-existence cases are based on a novel interpretation of the game as a backward stochastic differential equation. This lemma is applicable to various decision-making problems, such as irreversible investment, dividend distribution, and volatility induction.

This study explores the asymmetric leptoquark case, specifically the scenario where one leptoquark has a significantly different mass from the others. To analyze this, an asymmetric electron-positron collider with a distinct leptoquark mass range is proposed. In the study's initial stage, precise conditions for producing this pair via the asymmetric mechanism are established. Furthermore, it computes cross sections for pair production via the asymmetric mechanism and scalar-scalar-fermion couplings relevant to the color triplet leptoquark model. It also considers various design parameters for the collider, computing cross sections for viable configurations and estimating signal yields based on various asymmetric leptoquark mass combinations. It is concluded that an asymmetric collider with a relatively heavy leptoquark can be produced cost-effectively, making this approach an efficient use of resource-limited next-generation lepton colliders.

The two CI fine structure line intensity ratios in extreme starburst galaxies can provide valuable information about low-density molecular winds or a circumgalactic gas reserve. The CI fine structure emission ratios are particularly useful for detecting these phenomena as they exist in near thermal equilibrium. Based on observations of nine extremely luminous star-forming galaxies, the CI line emission ratios indicate that a significant portion of the CI gas has densities lower than $0.1 \text{ cm}^{-3}$, which is expected for material in the outer, low-density regions of these galaxies. The CI line emission ratio results align with a general model of extreme starburst galaxies featuring a central high-density region, a molecular wind with densities located in a range found in these galaxies, and possibly a large reservoir of circumgalactic gas with very low densities. The CI gas distribution in extreme starburst galaxies may offer new insights into their evolution and the origin of ultra-high energy galaxies.

Finding the largest overlapping region between two metric balls, defined by the Hamming distance, is a key step in coded caching systems with mutual information. For certain parameters, including a maximum of two differences in cache sizes, we derive an efficient algorithm to identify this intersection. Additionally, a larger intersection is found in the case of supersymmetric metric balls in an odd number of dimensions under 2k.
