This research presents a two-block ${{\rm{APD}}}$ algorithm for solving the ${{\rm{L}}}_1$-PCA problem after a rotational transformation, which is maintained throughout the solution process. Our proposed solution achieves an optimal solution with minimal norm through the introduction of a minimal-norm framework. This framework can be reduced to a two-block optimization problem, which is solved using a generalised alternating direction method of multipliers. A key feature of our approach is that it guarantees an optimal solution from the variable update stage. Our method demonstrates superior performance in terms of solution accuracy and computational efficiency when compared to other two-block reformulation methods. Notably, our algorithm outperforms the standard ${{{\rm{ADMM}}}}$ algorithm in terms of convergence speed and computational efficiency. Finally, a global convergence theorem is established for our algorithm, which is also demonstrated through various numerical experiments and comparative analyses.

The process of semantic labeling involves several steps, including verifying the consistency of the annotated data. In this approach, a paraphrasing task is employed to produce a table that lists possible relations between words that are intended to be antonyms, leveraging existing labeled data to validate the consistency of the antonym relationships. This is achieved by training a BERT-based parser to extract these relations from the data, with a key assumption being that complex, high-quality datasets leave "fingerprints" that reflect the consistency of the annotated labels. To generate the target table, three methods are used: a self-consistency check, a pairwise check, and a k-way check. The paper presents a dataset called SemAnt, which is designed to evaluate the validity of the consistency checks for the purpose of improving large-scale semantic labeling.

Our new method called HiTMap represents a innovative way for autonomous vehicles to navigate efficiently. This approach combines the benefits of place-based and global metric maps by using a hierarchical2metric framework. HiTMap enables precise navigation through a metric map sections while simultaneously managing large-scale navigation with a graph of map section locations. To achieve this, we developed a novel global metric map section layout representation that segments the metric map into distinct sections, each with its own local map. These sections are then organized into a hierarchical structure consisting of individual sections, clusters of sections, and ultimately a global overview. We demonstrate the effectiveness of HiTMap in a complete end-to-end system on the autonomous driving task, achieving superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods. This is achieved through learning HiTMap using solely video data from the vehicle sensor suite in a unsupervised manner.

Using a two-loop Rabi process in a atomic interferometry system, we simulate the detection of a weak local magnetic field that varies quickly in time and is confined to a small area. Sensitivity analysis indicates that even minor, localized field variations can be detected with high precision - as small as one percent in amplitude with a millimeter scale and variations occurring within a few seconds can be identified with a grating pulse sequence that matches the precision of the atomic interferometer. These findings are relevant for atomic clocks that use Rabi cycles, and they demonstrate the potential of atomic interferometry to study sub-lab-scale features, including the Sachs-Wolfe and Sunyaev-Zeldovich effects in the cosmic microwave background.

We illustrate that a straightforward approach to modeling data subsets, unrelated to their origins, results in spinoffs from the fields of mixture models and clustering that have profound implications. Specifically, directing our nonparametric method on a set of distinguishable admixture components leads to advancements in cluster analysis that are both informative and beneficial. Conversely, placing a Dirichlet process prior on density distributions yields a primary benefit in identifying unique, identifiable admixture weights in the form of permutable estimates that can be directly mapped to individual data points, effectively resolving the perplexing problem of assigning cluster probabilities. A working model for the first scenario is demonstrated through the use of the Infinite Gaussian Mixture model, while clustering analysis is examined in detail. The second model is explored through the Infinite Nested Dirichlet Process in relation to nested clustering.

GPU simulation tools struggle with real-time performance due to inefficient memory allocation methods. Developing a memory allocator that maximizes GPU memory usage without compromising speed or safety is challenging, as it depends on specific application requirements. Many simulation tools try to combine features of several allocators, but this approach consumes memory and time, as it requires multiple memory pools. We created DynaSOAr, an innovative GPU memory allocator designed to manage memory efficiently, safely, and quickly like the system default, while also enabling multiple memory pools to coexist without overlap. DynaSOAr leverages CUDA Stream technology to enhance performance for multiple pools on separate CUDA Streams, and was tested on 9 time-sensitive applications, demonstrating significant speed improvements of up to 14.4% compared to alternative solutions.

We investigate the influence of magnetic adatoms and dimer in aluminum, both single and paired, on the characteristics of a state known as "shy" by analyzing the spectral properties of Al(111).  By utilizing angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), we calculate the impacts of various magnetic configurations on the YSR peaks.  The theory calculations reveal that the peak positions in systems with a single magnetic adatom, systems with a dimer in various arrangements are essentially identical and unaffected by the spin-orbit interaction.  Furthermore, when considering a dimer with a specific separation in systems with a strong magnetic moment, we find that the peak positions can shift and merge, which may be observable through ARPES experiments.  This distinctive response to the magnetic properties and provides a characteristic signature that can help identify the origin of magnetic vortices observed in superconducting samples with embedded magnetic impurities, as well as offer a theoretical explanation for the magnetic dimers also observed in these systems.

A comprehensive study of a complex and varied star system with multiple planets transiting is presented, although relatively rare compared to single-transiting planets. A specific cluster of recently identified transiting mini-Neptunes, found in that system, offers an opportunity to better understand their commonality and distribution. A method is described that utilizes the location of these planets within a star's environmental range, known as the habitable zone, along with additional data from the star and planetary system to evaluate their characteristics. A notable example of this analysis is found in the LHS 3844 system, where none of the planets are located within the habitable zone, yet there is potential for a second, unidentified transiting planet that could exist.

The electronic structure of carbon and nitrogen defects in stoichiometric rutile TiO2 has been thoroughly examined through all-first-principles calculations. The study reveals that both C and N defects prefer to replace Ti atoms, with neutral C defects exhibiting a spin state of 1 and a magnetic moment of approximately 1.5 $\mu_B$, while neutral N defects exhibit a spin state of 2 and a magnetic moment of approximately 2 $\mu_B$. The valence band maximum in these systems is composed primarily of carbon or nitrogen 2s and 2p states, respectively. Notably, the (001) surface of TiO2 is less stable than the (110) surface, yet it displays a lower defect formation energy, particularly for C and N defects with low coordination numbers. Furthermore, highly coordinated C and N defects in TiO2 display deep magnetic states, whereas less coordinated variants exhibit shallow, mostly nonmagnetic characteristics. Compared to experimental measurements, our calculated defect charging levels and transition levels show reasonable agreement, although some discrepancies remain for certain configurations.

Top-quark decays into other flavor is a rare occurrence dictated by the Standard Model's quantum mechanical 'mixing', and extending this investigation to $t\rightarrow d^{0}b$ and $t\rightarrow s0b$ processes, which involve changing flavor without changing charge, is a significant challenge. Using ATLAS experimental data with a total mass of 37.4~GeV from 139~GeV proton-proton collisions, where the top quark was reconstructed in the $t\rightarrow Wb\rightarrow \ell\nu b$ channel, branching ratio upper limits were derived for the aforementioned processes. Specifically, the limits for $t\rightarrow d^{0}b$ and $t\rightarrow s0b$ decays were found to be less than 5.9x10$^{-4}$ and 4.0x10$^{-4}$, respectively, representing the current most precise results obtained without considering new, exotic phenomena. Additionally, branching ratio limits were also obtained for flavor changing neutral processes $t\rightarrow Zb$ and $t\rightarrow \gamma b$, which have a charged particle emission probability of nearly 10$^{-3}$, consistent with previous research findings.

A key consequence of a dual formulation of a dual problem yields an infinite-dimensional linear programming basis that is further constrained by a natural combinatorial edge-coloring problem with a lower bound of $2r/(r-f_r)$ for edge-coloring with a graph having a graph property $F$ whose coloring is not proper, specifically when the graph is embedded in a graph with a graph property $F$. This result, previously known for specific instances, is proven for the case when $f_r$ is equal to one. Follow-up research builds on this finding by considering a combinatorial edge-coloring problem with a lower bound of $r/(r-f_r)$ in the case of an infinite girth and circumference, which is a lower bound for edge-coloring with a graph having a graph property $F$ even after restricting to subgraphs with a graph property $F$ for any coloring scheme. This is in contrast to the classic Szemeredi's theorem, which states that for any constant, there exists a corresponding graph with a graph property $F$-coloring that is not colorable with a graph having a graph property $F$-coloring.

A significant factor affecting the precise determination of mass in bound states under the influence of a confining potential A/r is irreducible uncertainty, which A/r's increasing intensity exacerbates. To minimize this effect's influence, the current study proposes conducting mass measurements with a particle-qubit (or qudit) system under the influence of the confining operator, particularly when the qudit system is finite. The tolerance to noise in mass determination is analyzed for various error channels (dephasing, amplitude damping, and bit-flip) and particle-qudit system combinations, demonstrating that determining the mass with a qutrib system is less susceptible to noise than a qubit system, provided the error channel is amplitude damping or dephasing, although bit-flip errors result in the qubit system being more robust. Notably, the degree of uncertainty in mass determination can be limited to a value greater than (A/r) for the error-free case.

Recent measurements indicate that the polarization of a positron beam is around 10%, 
which is insufficient for several desired applications, including the creation of laser
wakefield-generated table-top positron beams. We have discovered a method to increase
positron polarization to greater than 30% using a simple and cost-effective spin
filtering technique employed in a thick target. This achievement is particularly notable
given the simplicity of our approach.

We establish that all groups with polynomial diameter possess finite conjugacy classes, notably including the existence of a bound on the number of nilpotent subgroups of a specific rank within these groups.

This research develops a high-sensitivity temperature detection method for implantable devices, where even minute changes in body temperature can indicate illness. Traditional approaches use precise, expensive components, which are inappropriate for small, low-power devices. Our proposed design achieves better results with a less precise frequency reference, allowing for more flexible integration. The sensor resolves and corrects temperature fluctuations of 10m{\deg}C and 5m{\deg}C, respectively, with a resolution of 1m{\deg}C, compared to typical specifications.

Given a topological stack and a topological groupoid, we develop the theory of topological groupoid extensions over it, which helps us understand the relationship between the category of such extensions and the integral pairing within a specific pairing value. Additionally, we investigate the concept of continuous sections within a specific fiber of a certain map related to these extensions, which can be expressed as a specific type of continuous section within a stack-valued function, this function consisting of a product of the input variable and a specific torsion fiber.

We investigated the mass development of molecular cores using the ALMA observatory, in an effort to clarify the formation process of massive stars.  We analyzed 1400 ALMA data sets in search of $^{13}$CO emission and measured the masses of cores, even those not yet associated with observable gas tracers like $^{13}$CO.  A mass growth rate of 0.04 Msun/year was found for cores leading up to the formation of massive stars, which is significantly slower than the rate of 0.1-0.9 msun/year observed during the protostellar phase.  Furthermore, we discovered a growth rate of 0.14 Msun/year for protostars formed from a low density gas reservoir, which is higher than expected based on previous research.  This discrepancy suggests additional factors influencing mass growth rates that we need to consider.

We investigate whether the operation of classical differentiation and integration preserving positive definiteness holds for zonal functions across all distances in d-dimensional space. Our study builds upon earlier findings and utilizes the method of generating functions to analyze this issue. Notably, our approach leads to a criterion for determining when the matrix formed by the cosine of angles between k unit vectors in R^d is positive definite for all possible combinations of these vectors. This criterion, in turn, contributes to an explicit formula for the coefficient of a specific term in an expansion of the inverse modified Bessel function of the second kind.

Our study delves into a range of behaviors observed in liquid foams, with a focus on their relationship to the roughness factor, which is the ratiotwo times the foam's liquid-to-solid ratio divided by the solid phase's packing ratio. A theoretical model with adjustable parameters is used to recover key behaviors seen at low and high roughness factors from the same equation of state and potential function. Notably, this model can replicate the gas ratio's dependence on the roughness factor as demonstrated in previous experiments and a more complex model. Moreover, it derives an analytical expression for the surface ratio with respect to the roughness factor, which matches a prior finding and has a large packing ratio limit that diverges, as expected from the model's nature. Additionally, our study highlights the model's ability to describe the foam's transition from a crystalline to a amorphous state as it transitions from low to high roughness factors.

Recently, deep learning methods have produced significant advances in the field of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image classification. A key factor contributing to the superior performance of state-of-the-art CNNs is the use of ensemble techniques, which involve combining multiple model instances through methods of training, parameter sharing, or arrangement. To effectively leverage parallel computing resources and deliver enhanced performance, this survey explores various ensemble strategies for CNNs and provides an comprehensive summary of innovative ensemble methods employed in recent state-of-the-art CNN ensembles.

A mathematical model is used to represent the rotating Hele-Shaw cell problem, taking into account the membrane tension that significantly impacts the stability of various states. Analytical solutions are obtained for low tension scenarios through a perturbation approach, while numerical methods are applied to scenario's that cannot be analytically solved. The analysis of the fundamental state shows its stability conditions in relation to tension, and the side branches' role in triggering the roll-up instability is highlighted. The interaction between the rotation-induced flow and membrane tension's influence on instability is also highlighted through our findings.

A detailed analysis of cyclopentadiene (C5H3) and its stability, based on the Ab initial Gordon-Kewshsh scheme, has been conducted and compared with the bi-stable nature of cyclobutadiene. The abundance of C5H3 in the circumstellar medium has been scrutinized and found to out-rank cyanogen derivatives of Cc cyclopentadiene by a factor of 5, given the lower energy barrier of CCH over CN derivatives. The abundance ratio of C5H3 over CN derivatives of Cc is given the symbol R(c) and is estimated to be between 4.86 and 5.06 for Cc greater than 5. The influence of the number of carbon atoms on the CN abundance has been found to be grafted onto the Cc distribution, given the abundance of the parent ion Cn+. The impact of cyclopentadiene on the ratio of N/C in the mass spectrum has been analyzed and found to be 16 times greater for Cc greater than 5. The potential for using the (CnN)/ (CnCN) system to measure the value of the mass-dependent fractionation exponent gamma has been proposed, with predicted values of 1.50 and 1.44 for the (CN)/ (CnCN) and (N)/ (CnN) ratios, respectively.

Our research focuses on enhancing neural machine translation by drawing inspiration from human language interpretation, specifically in how listeners use 'look-ahead' to anticipate upcoming context. To this end, we developed a novel approach called Look-Ahead Attention (LA-Atm). This approach allows the model to access future context by utilizing multiple parsing paths, which are then filtered to produce a context that is both efficient and contextually relevant. Our experiments employed the LA-Atm in conjunction with the standard attention-based translator, utilizing public evaluation datasets for the task of end-to-end neural machine translation. The results demonstrate that LA-Atm leads to significant improvements across various evaluation metrics, particularly in scenarios involving phrasal and morphological translation. Morphological aspects of the target language proved challenging for the (look-ahead) attention model.

This week's lecture will focus on interpreting a complex technical concept, in this case grid computing, from a translational perspective. This method involves effectively conveying such specialized knowledge across diverse contexts and audiences, a process that necessarily includes incorporating it into broader societal and cultural frameworks. This perspective will be supported by concrete examples related to the development of grid computing technology and its subsequent application in a medical context specifically cancer treatment.

A lambda-scalar field Friedmann model is presented as a new approach to describe early cosmic inflation, where the model's inflation behavior is determined by a power-law function of energy density, analogous to Ericksen's formula from fluid dynamics. Both single-field and two-field versions of the model are analyzed, and it is shown that they can effectively replicate observations of a specific spectrum and cosmic perturbation phase. Furthermore, the model can explain the cosmic Hoster parameter in relation to inflationary energy, although it requires an extremely low-viscosity coefficient to do so. Additionally, an idealized, non-gravitating singlet scalar field model is examined, and its lambda-dependent equations are derived, categorized, and solved in each category to obtain corresponding energy density expressions.

We employ the knowledge from dark sector theories, specifically hidden sector models, to re-examine the experimental data from the $J/$$\psi$ meson invisible decay process. By utilizing the $J/$$\psi$ meson production cross section, we can derive limits on dark matter scattering off nucleons, which serves as a universal reference for direct detection experiments. In the context of Chiral Lagrangian Effective Field Theory, we establish more stringent constraints on dark matter-nucleon scattering than the existing ASH and COSMA experiments, which are capable of providing unprecedented probing of the weakly interacting dark matter paradigm with nucleon scattering cross section thresholds as low as $\sim$10$^{-41}$ cm$^2$ for masses $\sim$ GeV.

MFSSA can be adapted to various practical scenarios, including temporal and spatial data analysis, by incorporating correlation coefficients into its objective function. This modification allows the method to focus on significant features while downplaying the impact of less relevant information. We have validated this enhanced model using synthetic data representing temperature patterns and a dataset comprising remote sensing images with a specific area of interest and corresponding temperature maps. Furthermore, by integrating this improved MFSSA variant with an autocorrelation-based criterion, we have developed a robust blind source separation framework tailored for spatial-temporal datasets. This new method, referred to as MS^2</tex>$, successfully reconstructs the underlying factors from observed data by minimizing a combined cost function. Numerical experiments have demonstrated the efficacy of this proposed approach in accurately restoring high-quality images and temporal sequences.

We analyze random walks consisting of i.i.d. increment variables with a specific weight function that varies based on the walk's current position. If the integral of this function is non-zero, we determine the asymptotic distribution of these walks in accordance with how this integral compares to the walk's variance. Such distributions include both the standard normal distribution and a two-sided exponential distribution. Such models are widely used in different fields, including the study of heavy traffic queues, and we derive our results using both summing a series of weierstrass functions and path functional methods.

A key factor in developing and improving plasma sources is understanding how key indicators such as electron temperature, density, and plate potential are distributed. This study employs a model based on self-consistent equations to analyze parameters of interest in an intricate plasma component, considering various sources' effects. By examining this component in isolation from others in a complex device allows for an in-depth analysis of critical factors affecting plate current and potential. To facilitate an accurate assessment of electron distribution and temperature, a numerical method was used to process a set of equations involving current balance and empirical laws of electron mobility and sheath drop. To validate the proposed method, the set of this study is compared with a more comprehensive model. The obtained results offer a detailed understanding of temperature and density patterns within the plate vicinity and the factors affecting potential and current behind the plate.

A newly proposed W-shaped network called ANet is effective for automatic nucleus detection in images. With a design that reduces redundancy and enhances information flow, ANet delivers superior performance and computational efficiency. By combining insights from pyramidal structures and skip connections, ANet outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially in handling large images. The network's efficiency is further demonstrated by its significantly lower parameter count and computational cost compared to other high-performance approaches. ANet's robustness and adaptability are further showcased in its successful application to images of different magnifications.

We prove that for representations with identical rank of twist-associated local gamma factors, in the cases of odd-dimensional special orthogonal and symplectic representations, they are isomorphic provided they share the same central character. This result paves the way for applying the Langlands-Siegel method and local-global duality for GL1 to establish a generalized converse to the local Gross-Prasad conjecture in specific settings.

Recently, graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have gained significant attention for their successful application in labeling nodes within complex networks across various domains. GCNs extend the principles of traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks (NNs), allowing them to be viewed as special cases of GCNs. We introduce a novel unified training framework that incorporates traditional CNNs and fully connected NNs alongside graph-based operations, enabling seamless integration and comparison of their respective forward and backward propagation mechanisms. This unified framework is flexible enough to accommodate different GCN variants and allows for the development of hybrid networks that combine local and global features. Through straightforward mathematical derivations, it is shown that traditional CNNs and fully connected NNs can be reparameterized to mimic the behavior of GCNs, and vice versa, by adjusting their respective operations. Furthermore, empirical evidence from image and web knowledge graph node classification tasks confirms that a network trained using this unified approach achieves superior performance.

We investigate the thermodynamic properties of hairy black holes resulting from the Maxwell-Chern-Simons gravity theory, deriving both their entropic and thermal stability characteristics. Particularly, in the context of rotating black holes, we find that the Chern-Simons term does not influence the entropic properties, which exclusively reflect those of standard Chern-Simons theory of pure gravity. Moreover, analyzing the thermodynamic stability of these hairy black holes reveals that they exhibit stable phases under specific parameter ranges, which are influenced by the Chern-Simons coupling.

Ultrasound elastography is a precise method for imaging tissue stiffness, but its accuracy is reduced by the difficulty of estimating lateral displacements. A more accurate method is possible using optical coherence tomography elastography, but it is slow for full-elastography tasks, limiting its medical imaging potential. A novel, fast approach combining elastography and acceleration is presented, utilizing ultrasound to measure tissue displacement in the vertical axis and OCT to estimate lateral displacements. This method significantly reduces the data processing required for elastography, resulting in visualizations of stiffness as little as 25 milliseconds, a substantial improvement from traditional techniques, while maintaining high-resolution imaging.

We introduce the concept of correctness for logical pseudocodes, distinguishing it from traditional pseudocode's accuracy. These logical frameworks can accurately reflect correct programs and safe pseudocodes, adhering to minimal safety precautions, in a setting where correctness cannot be guaranteed but desired outcomes can be enforced as correct. Our approach to calculating the difference between correct and incorrect results can be applied to a variety of meaningful outcomes, regardless of their nature. We demonstrate how this framework can be used to enforce correct outcomes of correct algorithms, and correct outcomes of correct and secure algorithms, respectively, and additionally, our approach yields a solution to the problem of correct pseudocode differing by a finite amount from correct and accurate pseudocode, respectively.

We present a one-pass coreset construction method for a dataset in high-dimensional space, specifically designed for the $k$-means clustering problem. Our approach achieves an approximation factor of $\mathcal{O}(\min\{k, d\})$ and involves maintaining a representative subset of size $\mathcal{O}(\frac{k\cdot \text{opt} + k^2\cdot \text{polylog}(k,d))$ with a squared distance sum threshold of $\mathcal{O}(\kappa\cdot \text{opt})$. Our method improves upon the current best one-pass coreset result, which features a dimension-dependent factor rather than a factor related to the number of centers, and also provides the first one-pass CO$_2$-set solution.

We applied spatial partitioning techniques to continuous grid worlds for decision-making in a pursuit-evasion mark process, demonstrating significant value reduction through NMDP formulation. Our method divides the grid into distinct regions, each treated as an NMDP state, substantially cutting computational costs without substantial policy performance loss. Specifically, we handled large-scale grids of 20x20 and 30x30 by applying spatial partitioning, achieving an approximate NMDP solution with reduced state spaces of 510 and 900 respectively, and implementing the policy for 20x20 grid within 1 minute. Our findings suggest addressing large-scale grids under HJ equation dynamics can be accomplished via NMDP decision-making process.

The behavior of high-energy PDFs for W and Z bosons, particularly the universal correction term of O\xi^2, is closely related to a process known as charge asymmetry in the diagonal component of dilepton production. This process occurs in collisions between protons and anti-protons at the Fermilab Tevatron and European Large Hadron Collider, where a part of the anti-proton collides with a proton at right angles. The part of the anti-proton is primarily composed of sea anti-quarks, while the PDF for W^- bosons exhibits a distinct shape compared to W^+ bosons, which consist mainly of u-type quarks. This discrepancy is responsible for the observed asymmetry in the scattering angles of the anti-lepton and lepton in the produced dileptons. The part that anti-proton has a significant impact on the calculation of the scattering asymmetry, which can be extracted from the analysis of these collisions.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, it is common to employ a single model that captures all task dynamics. While this approach works well when tasks are similar, using one model for diverse tasks can lead to confusion and poorer performance on any given task. To address this, we propose "Learn to Learn Multiple Dynamics Models" (L2MD), which allows the agent to master a set of task-specific dynamics models. In addition to learning multiple models, the agent also acquires the ability to select the most appropriate model for each state, minimizing performance loss when the appropriate model is not available. Our proposed method is evaluated through the (G)OFA benchmark, which shows that L2MD significantly improves performance, particularly when simpler methods like (G)OFA are forced to use one model for all tasks.

In 1935, George Rosser enhanced Gregory Godel's first incompleteness theorem by proving that if a formal system is capable of basic arithmetic and is consistent, then it either has an infinite number of statements that cannot be proven or false within that system, or it does not accommodate basic arithmetic. For simpler consistent systems, the statement that cannot be proven becomes one that cannot be falsified. This statement is known as the Rosser sentence, which is closely related to the Godel sentence of the system. If the system is consistent but does not accommodate basic arithmetic, the Rosser sentence and Godel sentence may both be true and falsifiable. This paper demonstrates the relationship between the Rosser sentence and Godel sentence using a concept called the diagonal degree of a system's consistency, which is an extension of Godel's diagonal method and the concept of diagonal degrees introduced by S. Cramer.

A generalized version of Hadamard's three circles theorem is proven for monogenic functions in multiple dimensions by deriving the upper bound of the geometric mean of their circumscribed spheres as a function of n. A new proof of the monogenic property of $1/(x-a)$ for dimensions greater than two is also presented.

Imaging applications often require going beyond just predicting the most probable outcome, as users need a range of possible solutions along with their respective probabilities. This is where Bayesian estimation becomes highly valuable, although traditional GAN-based methods fall short in emulating a posterior distribution when likelihoods are difficult to compute. In response, we've developed a novel, Bayesian-friendly formulation that allows for regularized conditional GANs to be trained effectively, thanks to the conditional architecture's convenience. Building on this foundation, we've also developed a regularized variant for non-invertible prior encoders that allows samples to be generated with desired utility regularization. Our theory is supported by experimental results using diverse low-light image denoising cases and a historical dataset, and can be applied to other image restoration tasks.

This research focuses on the assessment of linear subspaces within fractional order systems to identify linear subspaces that maintain their linearity given a specific fractional order, and on the characterization of these subspaces. It first examines the kernel and image of the operator associated with the fractional differential in order to determine all linear subspaces that are invariant. Furthermore, it utilizes this kernel-image representation to evaluate the algorithm for detecting linear subspaces in fractional order systems.

Recent observations of the radio pulsar PSR B1133+16, conducted using the Arecibo Observatory, have revealed the plasma environment through the analysis of radio wave scintillation.  By examining the time-dependent changes in scintillation, researchers were able to determine that the pulsar's emission was being scattered by the Earth-screen interstellar medium.  This study identified 3 distinct areas of this medium, consisting of individual layers of this medium.  These areas, located 50 pc, 85 pc, and between pc from us, were found to be responsible for most of the time-dependent scintillation observed at 4.3 GHz.  By analyzing the individual characteristics of these areas, researchers have been able to create an accurate model of this medium, opening the possibility of using this phenomenon as an interstellar probe.  Such a probe could examine the structure of this medium, provide an absolute measurement of its distribution, and even detect nearby areas of this medium that do not significantly affect most of our observations.

This paper proposes a method for modeling quasi-periodic signals, including speech and other signals with periodic patterns, by combining a cascaded network of convolution recurrent networks. In each stage of this design, the network extracts the periodic component from the residual signal, which contains varying amplitude and frequency modulations. By utilizing shared weights and operations for extracting the periodic component, we can efficiently train this model even for large acoustic datasets. When applied to smaller signals, it demonstrates significant performance improvements, and when trained on large datasets, it delivers state-of-the-art results for speech recognition with minimal modification of the model.

Using the theory of topological Hochschild homology as a topometric
equivalent to the classical formula $H_{*}(\mathrm{BC}(\mathcal{C}),\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{C})) \cong \mathrm{TC}^{-}(\mathcal{C})$,
we identify $\mathrm{TC}^{-}(\mathcal{C})$ in the bicategorical context with a specific "shadow" of the bicategory $\mathcal{C}$.

The VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) benchmark, comprising 11 distinct sounds across the complete frequency spectrum at sampling rates up to 48kHz, has been created to assess the robustness of models to signal processing effects. This benchmark processes low-budget signal processings effects, including those common in consumer electronics and social media messaging applications. Notably, it examines consumer-grade equipment for signal recording and digital processing, as well as analog processing that influences the spectral characteristics of signals. When processed through recording devices, VGG-SS demonstrates that models trained on it maintain source identification accuracy even for signals with narrow bandwidth, and it reveals sources with the highest consumption-device recording difficulty, including the Bose SoundLink Mini. VGG-SS provides training data for models that accurately reflect real-world conditions, allowing for precise estimates of performance when deploying these models on mobile devices with limited resources. This includes an analysis of the impact of various signal processing effects on source identification accuracy, demonstrating that it retains high source identification accuracy despite processing effects that are prevalent in consumer electronics and social media messaging apps.

Existing hyperbolic graph convolutional networks (GCNs) based on the hyperbolic distance metric are limited in their ability to perform convolution operations while preserving the inherent geometry of graph data. This restriction arises from the loss of parent relationship information in affine models, which is crucial for determining a node's position within its parent's hypersphere. To address this challenge, we propose a novel network architecture called the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that utilizes the Lorentzian distance model. LGCN overcomes the constraint of GCNs by enabling GCN-like convolution operations without distorting the hyperbolic geometry. Furthermore, LGCN enhances the representational capacity of GCNs by incorporating additional features. Extensive experiments conducted across four hyperbolic graph datasets and six tasks related to node classification and link prediction demonstrate the superior performance of LGCN in comparison to existing hyperbolic GCNs.

This research focuses on the inverse problem of determining a time-varying source term in a fractional diffusion equation, derived from measurements within a specific domain. To facilitate the analysis, we first establish an observability inequality for the adjoint problem, leveraging which we then prove that solutions to the PDE exhibit stability, characterized by bounded displacement in both measure and exponentiation.

The concept of equilibrium in social systems is ambiguous, suggesting that these systems may operate under non-equilibrium conditions. This could potentially explain why many observable characteristics of social systems are described using non-Boltzmann probability distributions. We propose interpreting the "state of equilibrium" in such systems as a quasi-equilibrium, resulting in distributions that align with the principles of non-equilibrium statistical mechanics. To demonstrate this theory, we adapt a variation of the Knuth game known as "Reversal" to represent a discrete-time financial market. By developing a stochastic model of this game and applying both equilibrium and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, we find that the system satisfies the maximum entropy principle under constraints, ultimately showing that the distribution of scores in the game follows a Tsallis distribution $q \approx 1$.

Starting from the action for linearized gravity with a gravitational eddy-current term and a mass term, we calculate the gravity pseudotensor and polarization states. By deriving the equations of motion from the combined action of gravitational fields and the pseudotensor, we find that adding a mass term influences two out of three degrees of freedom directly and indirectly, while the pseudotensor's expression shows a direct influence from the mass term in one of the three degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we combine our results with those of other researchers to obtain expressions for the gravitational eddy-current term and mass term pseudotensors. However, unlike the General Relativity pseudotensor, these terms cannot be eliminated through coordinate transformations. Consequently, it is concluded that due to its linearized Einstein-Podolsky-Dirac equation of motion, a linearized gravitational field with a mass term exhibits three degrees of freedom.

Quantum statistical mechanics is organized into four equilibrium states under Hamiltonian dynamics: thermal equilibrium described by the canonical ensemble, classical or microcanonical equilibrium, and nonequilibrium states represented by the Wigner function in phase space. A general framework for both closed and open quantum systems is proposed to achieve this. The canonical ensemble results from applying a sudden approximation to the canonical environment, while the microcanonical ensemble arises from applying the same approximation to the system itself. The Wigner function nonequilibrium state is achieved through a sudden nonequilibrium process.

To infer a two-level system's negative temperature, a novel, straightforward experiment employs a single photon whose upper and lower states constitute the two levels. This system achieves equilibrium at a temperature that can be expressed as a fraction of infinity, as indicated by the equality of its state probabilities. Comparatively, the absolute temperature scale typically starts from zero for the coldest possible temperature and extends to infinity before entering a two-stage system that includes negative temperatures and culminates at plus or minus infinity.

We propose an extension of the Standard Model that includes both type I seesaw and dark parity symmetry, giving it consistency at high energies. This model features a minimal dark sector consisting of a complex scalar singlet, with the goal of maintaining the vacuum stability, the see-saw mechanism, and dark parity symmetry. We analyze the impact of this approach on the dark matter relic abundance, assuming that the scalar doublet obtains its mass from the Higgs portal and contributes to type I seesaw. By exploring the implications of our framework, we examine the dark matter abundance, the effective neutrino mass, the Higgs potential, and the effects of thermal and non-thermal processes. To achieve the desired level of the neutrino mass, this model requires the introduction of the type IV seesaw mechanism. Our study reveals that this model can be consistent with up to $10^{13}$ GeV, result in the dark matter abundance of $\Omega_{\rm DM} h^2 \sim 0.12$, and exceed the effective neutrino mass constraint of $0.17$ eV. Furthermore, our study includes the effect of the neutrino production via the oscillation of the dark matter component and the effects of thermal processes.

We present a comprehensive study of mean-field and beyond for a d^2 system in 
crystalline structures with large interaction potentials and meV-scale crystal field 
separation, encompassing both ferro- and antiferro- magnetic configurations. 
Despite being prohibitively expensive for full quantum Monte Carlo simulations, 
these oxymetalllic compounds are ideal for an accurate treatment using the Gutzwiller 
variational approach. 
Our analysis involves deriving the effective spin-orbit coupling constant by comparing the 
Gutzwiller and exact diagonalization results, which is possible due to the feasibility 
of full quantum Monte Carlo calculations. 
We investigate the phase diagram of the model under different crystal field separtion 
and interaction strengths for both cases and find that the effective spin-orbit 
coupling constant exhibits a non-monotonic behavior with the crystal field splitting, 
which can lead to either enhanced or suppressed spin-orbit effects compared to the 
bare parameter, with implications for finding materials with engineering spin-orbit 
coupling strengths.

To establish a connection with recent findings by Carrell, Sheshadri, and Zewiet, this research examines the fundamental $i$-functions of toric complete intersections embedded in varieties defined by equations with constant coefficients. When the toric variety and the embedding are smooth, we prove that the relative $i$-functions of the toric complete intersection can be expressed in terms of the relative $i$-functions of the surrounding toric variety. Additionally, the fundamental $i$-functions of the toric complete intersection can be described using a system of differential equations derived from Griffiths' theory.

A critical aspect of using deep neural networks for medical image analysis is ensuring reliable control over generated images' key features. While prior research has demonstrated the feasibility of performing this task, it is hindered by the complex constraint of training deep neural networks, even though simple methods of translation between conditions can affect the accuracy of disease representation. We propose a novel method of latent code modification that accounts for the accurate representation of medical conditions, enabling precise alteration of medical conditions while preserving the robustness of neural networks' training. Our approach, based on deriving a distance metric in the latent code space, allows changing medical conditions through neural network training only, and results show improved performance in segmenting images and classifying images with medical conditions through Neumann distance method application.

Humans struggle to visualize and analyze data beyond three dimensions, making this a significant challenge in various fields including science, medicine, and statistics. To address this difficulty, a new method called ViDaExpert, which leverages large language models, has been developed. This method utilizes a domain expert system to guide users through an interactive process, demonstrating each step of the explanation and allowing for feedback. By providing a clear, visual representation of high-dimensional data alongside a narrative, ViDaExpert simplifies the task of understanding and working with complex data. In evaluations conducted across three distinct scenarios, the method has been found to effectively guide users in navigating and making sense of high-dimensional data. Furthermore, recordings of the interactive sessions have been obtained, offering a resource for research purposes.
